1051.title: Mercy in power
1051.hook: the rulers people still speak of warmly are remembered for mercy
1051.howItsDone: Muslims often cite the hadith that each person is a shepherd responsible for a flock, and the Qur'an's praise of the Prophet's leniency, when speaking about how parents, employers and leaders should treat those in their care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ordinary believer: the sweeper of the mosque, kept in Sahih Muslim, and the mothers, farmers and traders who carried the faith. Your line was ordinary hands carried it. Who did you thank? Day one thousand fifty-one.

A parent at bedtime. A shift manager writing next week's schedule. A teacher holding a red pen over a failing paper. A referee with a whistle. A landlord reading a late-rent text. None of them is a sultan. All of them hold a little power over someone else, and every day they choose how to use it. This path has walked past a lot of rulers this year. Some built, some conquered, some fell. When you ask which of them people still speak of warmly, a pattern shows up, and it isn't the size of the army. Today: mercy in power.
screen: `A PARENT, A MANAGER, A REFEREE.` → `EVERYONE HOLDS A LITTLE POWER.` → `WHICH RULERS ARE SPOKEN OF WARMLY?`

segments.voice: Go back to two names from earlier this year. Salah al-Din, who retook Jerusalem and let its people ransom themselves and leave, instead of putting the city to the sword. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, who began his reforms with his own family's wealth. Neither story is told today for the size of an army. What people still retell is the mercy. Second, the Qur'an puts mercy at the root of leadership. After the battle of Uhud, when some of the Prophet's companions had failed him, a verse speaks to him, in Pickthall's translation: "It was by the mercy of Allah that thou wast lenient with them (O Muhammad), for if thou hadst been stern and fierce of heart they would have dispersed from round about thee." And then, in the same verse, it tells him to pardon them, to ask forgiveness for them, and to consult them. Not to punish. To keep them close and keep listening. Third, a hadith brings this down to every household. In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet, peace be upon him, says each of you is a shepherd, and each is responsible for the flock: the ruler for his people, a man for his family, a woman for her husband's household, a servant for what his master left in his care. Small power is still power. Fourth, another hadith, in Jami' at-Tirmidhi: the merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One above will be merciful to you. The red pen, the schedule, the whistle. Each one a small throne. And the history suggests what will be remembered from it.
screen: `SALAH AL-DIN AND UMAR: THE MERCY IS TOLD.` · `LENIENT, OR THEY WOULD HAVE SCATTERED.` · `EACH OF YOU IS A SHEPHERD.` · `THE MERCIFUL ARE SHOWN MERCY.` · then, large: `IT WAS BY THE MERCY OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: The practice: use your small power mercifully. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself one honest question: where do I hold a little power over someone? A child, an employee, a student, a younger sibling, a person waiting on a reply from you. Pick one. Picture them. Now picture the next moment you'll have a choice about them: a mistake to correct, a request to answer, a deadline to enforce. Don't drop the standard. Just see what a lenient answer would look like, the kind that keeps them close. Rest there until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Mercy in power. Leniency and pardon from the one who could punish, the thing people remember of their rulers. Today's word.
Your line: mercy is remembered. Today, when your small power meets someone's mistake, answer one notch gentler than you planned. Day one thousand fifty-one.

1052.title: Failures too
1052.hook: Muslim history includes cruelty and injustice, and the tradition itself criticizes it
1052.howItsDone: Muslims seek forgiveness (istighfar) from God daily, and the tradition teaches that wronging another person also requires putting it right with that person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mercy in power: the leniency the Qur'an praised in the Prophet, and the shepherd in every household. Your line was mercy is remembered. Where did you answer one notch gentler? Day one thousand fifty-two.

Who wrote down the day of Karbala? Not an enemy of Islam. Muslim historians did, al-Tabari among them, and they set down, in plain detail, an army of a Muslim ruler killing the Prophet's own grandson and many of his family. Names, speeches, who struck whom. They didn't bury it. They copied it, taught it, and argued over it. That's worth sitting with. This path has told a lot of history this year with admiration. Today it turns the other way, and asks what the tradition does with its own worst days. Today: failures too.
screen: `WHO WROTE DOWN KARBALA?` → `MUSLIM HISTORIANS DID.` → `THEY DIDN'T BURY IT.`

segments.voice: There were cruel rulers. Unjust wars. Prisoners mistreated, scholars jailed, the poor taxed to pay for palaces. Muslim history holds all of that, the way every long human history does. The surprising part is where the sharpest criticism came from: inside. First, the standard. The Qur'an asks believers to tell the truth even when it costs their own side. In Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred." Against yourselves. That includes your own dynasty and your own history. Second, the voice. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud calls a word of justice spoken before an unjust ruler the best kind of striving. Third, the people who paid for it. The scholar Ahmad ibn Hanbal was imprisoned and beaten under the caliph's officials for refusing to say what the court required. Hasan al-Basri, whom we met earlier, admonished the governors of his day. Their students kept their names and honored them; the officials who did the beating are mostly footnotes. Fourth, the mirror. In the Qur'an, Adam and his wife did wrong in the garden, and their answer is the model of an honest believer, in Pickthall's words: "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves." No excuses, no blaming the other. That's the lesson history leaves for a single life: the faith is strong enough to name its failures, and so is a person.
screen: `CRUELTY AND INJUSTICE HAPPENED.` · `STAUNCH IN JUSTICE, EVEN AGAINST YOURSELVES.` · `A WORD OF JUSTICE BEFORE A TYRANT.` · `OUR LORD, WE HAVE WRONGED OURSELVES.`

segments.voice: The practice: admit one failure. Settle, and breathe. Let one thing come up that you got wrong, recently or long ago. Not the worst thing you've ever done. Just one real one. A sharp word. A promise dropped. A time you took the easy side. Look at it straight, the way those historians looked at Karbala, without dressing it up and without beating yourself with it. Say it to yourself in one plain sentence: I did this. If you pray, you can say the words of Adam and his wife: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. The bell holds the time.
Failures too. Muslim history holds cruelty and injustice, and the tradition's own scholars and historians named them. Today's word.
Your line: honesty is faith. Today, if the failure you named touched someone, tell them so, in one plain sentence. Day one thousand fifty-two.

1053.title: Unsung women
1053.howItsDone: Muslim communities remember women such as Khadijah, Aisha and Fatimah from the Prophet's household, and local histories honor women who founded mosques, schools and charitable endowments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, failures too: the tradition naming its own worst days, and Adam and his wife saying we have wronged ourselves. Your line was honesty is faith. Did you say the plain sentence? Day one thousand fifty-three.

Mecca, a room within reach of the sanctuary. A woman sits with a book open in front of her. Across from her, men with pens and paper, scholars who traveled to be here. She reads Bukhari's collection of hadith aloud, line by line, and they copy it down, checking every word against what they hear, so that later they can say: I heard it from her. Her name is Karima al-Marwaziyya, and it went into the chain by which that book was passed on. Women were in this history the whole way through, often doing the work while someone else got the chapter. Today: unsung women.
screen: `A WOMAN READS; SCHOLARS WRITE.` → `I HEARD IT FROM HER.` → `THE WORK, WITHOUT THE CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an sets the frame. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! I suffer not the work of any worker, male or female, to be lost." The chronicles might drop a name; the verse says the work isn't dropped. So let's pick some back up, four kinds, all names this path has already met. First, a founder. In Fez, tradition says a woman named Fatima al-Fihri used her inheritance to found the mosque that became al-Qarawiyyin, a place of study. Second, a teacher: Karima, in that room in Mecca, a woman whose reading of Bukhari's collection men traveled to hear. Third, a poet. In Sokoto, Nana Asma'u wrote poems in several languages to teach the faith, and trained women teachers who carried those lessons to women in villages far from her. Fourth, a patron. Zubayda, wife of the caliph Harun al-Rashid, whose name tradition gives to the wells and stations of the pilgrim road from Iraq to Mecca, and other women after her who paid for schools, fountains and mosques with their own wealth, their names cut into a stone over a door that passersby rarely stop to read. Founders, teachers, poets, patrons. What ties them together is that the history needed them and often forgot to say so. The lesson for an ordinary day isn't only about the past. Look around any mosque, school or family today and ask who is doing work that nobody writes down.
screen: `NO WORKER'S WORK IS LOST, MALE OR FEMALE.` · `A FOUNDER: FATIMA AL-FIHRI IN FEZ.` · `A TEACHER AND A POET: KARIMA, NANA ASMA'U.` · `A PATRON: ZUBAYDA'S WELLS.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one woman's name. Settle, and breathe. Start with the names from today: Zubayda, Fatima, Karima, Asma'u. Say them slowly, one per breath. Then think closer to home. Who is the woman in your own story whose work made something possible and never got the credit? A mother who kept the house running, a teacher, an aunt who taught the prayers, a colleague who did the unseen part of a project. Say her name too, quietly, if you know it. If you don't, decide to find it out. The bell holds the time.
Unsung women. The founders, teachers, poets and patrons whose work built Muslim history, often without the credit. Today's word.
Your line: they were there. Today, learn the name of one woman behind something you use, a school, a mosque, a recipe, a road, and say it out loud once. Day one thousand fifty-three.

1054.title: One ummah, many faces
1054.hook: Arab, Persian, Turkish, African, Malay, Chinese, European
1054.howItsDone: Muslims of every background pray in the same rows, facing the Ka'ba in Mecca and reciting in Arabic, while keeping their own languages, dress, food and festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, unsung women: Zubayda's wells, Fatima in Fez, Karima teaching in Mecca, Nana Asma'u in Sokoto. Your line was they were there. Whose name did you learn? Day one thousand fifty-four.

Friday, in a big-city mosque. The row forms, shoulder to shoulder, feet touching. On the left, a taxi driver whose family came from Cairo. Next to him a student from Istanbul, then a grandfather from Lagos, a nurse whose parents came from Kuala Lumpur, a man from Xi'an with a white cap, a convert from Sarajevo, an engineer from Tehran. Different languages in the parking lot, different food at home, different ways of tying a headscarf or a turban. Then the imam says God is greatest, and every one of them raises their hands at once. Today: one ummah, many faces.
screen: `ONE ROW, SHOULDER TO SHOULDER.` → `CAIRO, ISTANBUL, LAGOS, KUALA LUMPUR.` → `ONE MOVEMENT.`

segments.voice: Ummah is the Arabic word for a community, a people, and Muslims use it for the whole worldwide community of believers. First, the Qur'an names it as one. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! this, your religion, is one religion, and I am your Lord, so worship Me." One religion. Second, the many faces were there among the Prophet's own companions. Bilal, of Abyssinian descent, gave his voice to the call to prayer. Salman came from Persia, searching for the truth. Suhayb, who grew up among the Byzantines, was called the Roman. The community around the Prophet, peace be upon him, was mixed before it was large. Third, the line that set the rule. In the sermon of the Prophet's last pilgrimage, as Musnad Ahmad reports it, he said no Arab is above a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab above an Arab, nor a light-skinned person above a dark-skinned one, nor the other way, except by piety. Rank by birth was cut off at the root. Fourth, what the history adds. This path has walked through Arab caliphs, Persian poets, Turkish sultans, West African scholars, Malay sultanates, Chinese mosques and the old Muslims of the Balkans. They prayed toward the same house in Mecca, in Arabic, and then went home and cooked their own food, sang their own songs and built in their own style. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari pictures believers as one body: when one part aches, the whole body feels it. One body. Many faces. The history suggests that's a feature, not a problem to fix.
screen: `ONE RELIGION, ONE LORD.` · `BILAL, SALMAN, SUHAYB: A MIXED CIRCLE.` · `NO ARAB ABOVE A NON-ARAB, EXCEPT BY PIETY.` · `ONE BODY, MANY FACES.`

segments.voice: The practice: appreciate a Muslim culture not your own. Settle, and breathe. Choose one place from today that you know least about: West Africa, Malaysia, China, Bosnia, Iran, Turkey, Egypt. Picture someone there right now, at the same prayer, saying the same Arabic words, in a room that looks nothing like yours. What are they wearing? What does the street outside sound like? What will they eat after? Hold them in mind until the bell, the way one part of a body feels another. If you pray, you can remember them in your next prayer. The bell holds the time.
One ummah. The worldwide community of Muslims: one religion, one direction of prayer, and every face, language and culture inside it. Today's word.
Your line: many faces. Today, try one thing from a Muslim culture you've never explored: a dish, a song, a poem, a photograph of a mosque. Day one thousand fifty-four.

1055.title: The prayer never stopped
1055.hook: empires rose and fell, and the five prayers went on
1055.howItsDone: Muslims pray five times a day at times set by the sun (dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night); travelers may shorten some prayers, and the sick may pray sitting or lying down.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one ummah: Bilal, Salman and Suhayb among the companions, and one row of many faces. Your line was many faces. What did you taste, hear or see from a culture new to you? Day one thousand fifty-five.

Try making a list of what's gone. The caliphs of Damascus. The caliphs of Baghdad. The courts of Cordoba and Cairo. Sultans, viziers, banners, coins with names nobody spends anymore. This path has spent a year watching them rise and fall. Now make the other list, of what's still here. It's shorter, and it's this: at dawn tomorrow, somewhere, someone will wash their face and hands and feet, stand on a mat, and say God is greatest. Then at noon. Then in the afternoon, at sunset, at night. The same five prayers people prayed under those rulers. Today: the prayer never stopped.
screen: `THE LIST OF WHAT'S GONE.` → `THE LIST OF WHAT'S STILL HERE.` → `FIVE TIMES, TOMORROW AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Why did the prayer outlast the empires? Start with how the Qur'an frames it. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." Fixed hours. Not tied to a palace, a capital or a king. Tied to the sun, which no dynasty owns. When a ruler fell, the sun still rose, and the time for dawn prayer still came. Second, the prayer was built not to stop. The Qur'an says that if you are in fear, you pray standing or on horseback, however you can, and when you're safe again you remember God as He taught you. Travelers shorten it. The sick pray sitting, or lying down. The form bends. The prayer doesn't break. Third, it was the Prophet's own last concern. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud records that among his last words, peace be upon him, was the prayer, the prayer, and care for those under your hand. Of all the things he could have left as final words, he pointed there. Fourth, look again at the history with that in mind. The prayer didn't depend on a caliph, so it didn't fall with one. A farmer's dawn prayer in a village never needed the court's permission. That's how a faith outlived its own empires, one person at a time, five times a day. And it's a lesson for any life that's going through its own rise and fall: a job ending, a move, an illness. The anchor that holds is the one that doesn't depend on the weather.
screen: `PRAYER AT FIXED HOURS, TIED TO THE SUN.` · `IN FEAR: STANDING OR ON HORSEBACK.` · `HIS LAST WORDS: THE PRAYER, THE PRAYER.` · `NO CALIPH NEEDED, SO NONE COULD END IT.` · then, large: `WORSHIP AT FIXED HOURS.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray on time today. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself which prayer comes next, and roughly when. Look at the light through the window, if there is one. Is the sun high, slanting, low, gone? That light is the prayer's clock. If you pray, decide now exactly where you'll be when the next prayer comes, and how you'll step away to pray it on time. If you don't pray, choose that moment anyway, and when it comes, stop for one breath and notice the light. The bell holds the time.
The prayer never stopped. Empires rose and fell, and the five daily prayers, tied to the sun, went on through all of it. Today's word.
Your line: the prayer went on. Today, keep the moment you chose, and when the time comes, step away from whatever you're doing and pray or pause. Day one thousand fifty-five.

1056.title: Returning to the source
1056.hook: renewers kept returning to the Qur'an and sunnah
1056.howItsDone: Muslims turn to the Qur'an and the sunnah as the final reference in matters of faith and practice, read through scholars and the schools of law that interpret them, and some read a portion of the Qur'an daily.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer never stopped: fixed hours tied to the sun, outlasting the courts. Your line was the prayer went on. Did you keep the moment you chose? Day one thousand fifty-six.

A river runs through a town. By the time it reaches the market it has picked up a lot along the way: soil from the fields, leaves, whatever the streets wash into it. Someone wants to know what the water was like at the start, and there are two ways to find out. Study it where it runs past you. Or walk upstream, past the town, past the fields, up into the hills, until you reach the spring where it comes out of the rock. The water there hasn't passed through anybody yet. This path has met a lot of reformers this year, in very different places and times. Look closely at what they did, and they keep walking upstream. Today: returning to the source.
screen: `A MUDDY RIVER THROUGH A TOWN.` → `FILTER IT, OR WALK UPSTREAM?` → `THE SPRING IN THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction is in the Qur'an itself. When believers disagree, in Pickthall's translation: "and if ye have a dispute concerning any matter, refer it to Allah and the messenger". In practice, for Muslims, that means the Qur'an and the sunnah, the example of the Prophet, peace be upon him. The source. Second, the Prophet framed it the same way. In the Muwatta of Imam Malik, he is reported to have said he left two things, and as long as people hold to them they won't go astray: the Book of God and his sunnah. Third, the history. We've met a hadith promising a renewer for the community at the head of every hundred years, and we've met the people later generations called renewers. Al-Ghazali named a work the Revival of the Religious Sciences. Shah Wali Allah of Delhi put the Qur'an into Persian so ordinary readers could reach it themselves. The reformers of Cairo urged Muslims to read the text again with open minds. Different centuries, different lands, the same direction: upstream. Fourth, an honest note. Renewers didn't agree on what they found at the spring. Some stressed the law, some the inner life, some education, some politics, and they argued with each other, sometimes bitterly. Many scholars hold that the schools of law and the long chain of teachers are how a believer reaches the spring safely, not silt in the river; others called for reading the sources more directly. Returning to the source didn't end the disagreement. It gave everyone the same place to stand while they had it. And it leaves a habit for a single life: when things get muddy, go back to the text itself, not someone's summary of it.
screen: `REFER IT TO ALLAH AND THE MESSENGER.` · `THE BOOK AND THE SUNNAH: TWO THINGS LEFT.` · `RENEWERS WALK UPSTREAM.` · `THEY DISAGREED AT THE SPRING, TOO.`

segments.voice: The practice: read a page of Qur'an. If you have one nearby, in Arabic or in translation, open it anywhere, or at the beginning. Settle, and breathe. Read slowly, a line at a time, as if no one had ever explained it to you. Don't hunt for meaning yet. Just let the words themselves come first. If you don't have one with you, say the opening surah to yourself, or simply its first line, in the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful, and listen to it as if for the first time. The bell holds the time.
Returning to the source. Renewal in Islam keeps going back to the Qur'an and the sunnah, upstream to the spring. Today's word.

1057.title: The Prophet's character
1057.hook: Aisha said his character was the Qur'an (Muslim)
1057.howItsDone: Muslims learn the Prophet's character from the Qur'an and the hadith collections, and many try to copy his everyday habits, such as smiling, helping at home and speaking gently, as part of following his sunnah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the renewers who kept turning back to the Qur'an and the sunnah. Your line was back to the source. Did you read a page, and did one line stay with you? Day one thousand fifty-seven.

A question, from a visitor who came to learn. A man named Sa'd ibn Hisham has come to Aisha, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, with a list of things he wants to understand. Somewhere in the list is the big one. Tell me about his character. What was he actually like? He might have expected a story, or a list of virtues, or a long description. Aisha answers him with a question of her own. Don't you read the Qur'an? Yes, he says. Then, she says, his character was the Qur'an. That short exchange, kept in Sahih Muslim, is where today begins.
screen: `TELL ME ABOUT HIS CHARACTER.` → `DON'T YOU READ THE QUR'AN?` → `HIS CHARACTER WAS THE QUR'AN.`

segments.voice: First, the word. In Arabic it's khuluq: character, disposition, the way a person habitually is. The same word sits in a verse addressed to the Prophet himself. Pickthall translates it: "And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature." Nature there is khuluq. So Aisha's answer points straight back to the book. Second, what her answer does. She doesn't hand Sa'd a portrait. She hands him a text he already owns. If you want to know the man, read what he lived by: the patience, the honesty, the mercy, the prayer at night. Some readers take her words in two directions at once. The Qur'an shows what his character was, and his life shows what the Qur'an looks like when a person actually does it. Third, the small evidence. The hadith collections keep ordinary moments, not only great ones. Asked what he did at home, Aisha said he kept busy serving his family, and when the call to prayer came he went out to pray. That's in Sahih al-Bukhari. Anas, who served him as a boy, said he served him for ten years and was never once told off with so much as a sigh of annoyance, never asked why did you do that. Bukhari keeps that too. And a saying in Tirmidhi counts a smile at your brother as charity. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary afternoon. A character is built from habits, and habits are small enough to copy. Nobody copies a whole life in a day. But one habit, a smile, a hand with the dishes, holding back the irritated sigh, can be tried before dinner.
screen: `KHULUQ: THE WAY A PERSON HABITUALLY IS.` · `SHE HANDED HIM A BOOK, NOT A PORTRAIT.` · `SMALL MOMENTS: HOME, A SERVANT, A SMILE.` · `HABITS ARE SMALL ENOUGH TO COPY.` · then, large: `AND LO! THOU ART OF A TREMENDOUS NATURE.`

segments.voice: The practice: choose one of his habits, and place it in your day. Settle, and let your breath slow. Three are in front of you. Helping at home without being asked. Holding back the sigh when someone gets something wrong. A real smile for someone you'll see today. Pick one. Now see where it happens: which room, which person, roughly what time. Walk through the moment once in your mind, doing it. If you pray, you can send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ before the bell, as Muslims do. If not, simply keep the picture of that one moment. The bell holds the time.
Khuluq, the Prophet's character and disposition, which Aisha said was simply the Qur'an lived out. Today's word.
Your line: his character was the qur'an. Today, do the one habit you chose, once, and notice how it lands with the person on the other end. Day one thousand fifty-seven.
